stories.headline: Governor Polis signs executive order to protect pollinators across Colorado
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis signed an executive order Wednesday directing state agencies to strengthen protections for bees and other pollinators, citing steep population declines driven by habitat loss, drought, invasive species and pesticide exposure. The order was signed at the Denver Zoo and includes three directives aimed at restoring pollinator habitats across Colorado.

The first directive calls on the Department of Natural Resources to collaborate with CDOT, the Colorado Department of Agriculture and other agencies to expand and restore pollinator-friendly habitat along roadsides and state-managed lands. The action builds on the 2024 Colorado Native Pollinating Insects Health Study, described as the most detailed account of pollinator health in the state's history.

Polis, who has worked previously as a beekeeper and online florist, said pollinators "touch everything we love about Colorado," underscoring the economic and ecological stakes for agriculture and natural ecosystems statewide. The executive order does not require legislative approval and takes effect immediately.

stories.headline: RTD board to consider overhaul of fare evasion enforcement, shift toward direct fines
stories.summary:
The Regional Transportation District board is set to vote on whether to direct staff to study replacing its education-first fare evasion approach with a system of direct administrative fines that RTD itself could collect. The proposal, sponsored by Board Secretary Chris Nicholson, was expected to be discussed at Wednesday's Operations, Safety and Security Committee meeting before heading to the full board for a vote Sept. 22.

Under current policy, RTD issues warnings far more often than citations — 12,789 warnings versus 1,096 citations in 2025, against nearly 5 million estimated rail fare checks. Nicholson argued that riders are now well-informed about fare requirements and that the education-first rationale no longer holds.

A key financial driver behind the proposal is that RTD currently receives none of the revenue from fare evasion citations, which are processed as class B traffic infractions through county courts. Nicholson pointed to other transit agencies that have moved enforcement in-house and seen higher compliance rates as a result.

If the board approves the study directive, staff would examine statutory changes, technology needs, equity considerations and public engagement plans, with a report due back to the board by February. RTD collects approximately $60 million annually in fare revenue.

stories.headline: Squirrels breach Castle Rock power substation, knock out electricity two days in a row
stories.summary:
Thousands of CORE Electric Cooperative customers in the south Denver metro lost power twice this week after squirrels entered a substation in Castle Rock on back-to-back days. The first outage, on Tuesday, affected about 4,400 members for more than two hours after a squirrel touched equipment and triggered a fault; Castle Rock officials described the incident as an explosion caused by the animal.

A second squirrel entered the same substation on Wednesday, damaging distribution equipment and causing a 40-minute outage for roughly 1,300 co-op members. Crews found animal remains that confirmed the cause, CORE spokesperson TJ Accola said, adding the cooperative could not confirm whether an explosion occurred Tuesday because no personnel were on site at the time.

Wildlife-related outages are a recurring challenge for CORE, accounting for between 5% and 10% of the co-op's annual outages, most involving birds or rodents. CORE crews cover most energized equipment and follow wildlife-protection guidelines, but Accola acknowledged that animals "continue to find new ways around even the best defense tactics."

stories.headline: Measles case confirmed in international visitor to Denver area; exposure sites identified
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment has confirmed a measles case linked to an international visitor who traveled throughout the state earlier this month, with several potential exposure sites identified across the Denver metro area. Health officials are urging anyone who may have visited the listed locations during the relevant time windows to monitor for symptoms.

Measles symptoms typically begin with fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, followed several days later by a rash that starts on the face and spreads downward. The CDPHE said it will continue to update its measles webpage as additional exposure information becomes available.

Measles is highly contagious and can spread to unvaccinated individuals who share a space with an infected person, even after that person has left. Residents who are unsure of their vaccination status are encouraged to contact their health care provider.

stories.headline: Optiv Security quietly relocates headquarters from Denver to Kansas, dealing blow to local tech sector
stories.summary:
Optiv Security, Colorado's leading cybersecurity firm, has moved its headquarters from downtown Denver to Leawood, Kan., without making a formal public announcement. The company has vacated its remaining space on floors 29 and 30 at 1144 15th St., a combined 39,415 square feet now listed for sublease through May 2031.

Optiv traces its Colorado roots to 2002, when Dan Burns founded Accuvant in downtown Denver. The company grew into a national cybersecurity provider before a 2014 merger with Kansas-based FishNet Security created Optiv, with Denver receiving the headquarters designation. The firm moved into the 15th Street tower in 2018 under a 15-year lease.

The departure follows Palantir's February relocation to Florida and comes as Denver's downtown office market continues to struggle with high vacancy rates. Optiv employs several hundred Colorado-based workers who will continue working remotely, and the company said Colorado remains a critical market.

The move adds to a pattern of major tech firms reducing their formal footprint in Denver even as remote employees remain in the region. Optiv's glowing rooftop sign above 15th and Arapahoe streets will remain, at least for now, as its sublease is marketed.

stories.headline: Littleton approves 30-year tax incentive to land Scheels sporting goods flagship store
stories.summary:
Scheels, the North Dakota-based sporting goods chain, will open a 300,000-square-foot store in Littleton after the city council approved a substantial incentive package Tuesday night. The store, projected to open in 2029, will be located at 700 W. Mineral Ave. as part of the Mineral Place mixed-use development on a 68-acre site where a large office complex once stood.

Under the agreement, Scheels will receive 54.67% of the sales tax it generates over 30 years, while developer Republic Investment Group will receive an additional 5.33% until it recoups $25 million for land and infrastructure contributions. Littleton retains 40% of sales tax revenue under the deal, which the city projects will generate $135 million in revenue in the store's first full year, rising to $200 million by year 10.

The store will be Scheels' 38th location and its third in Colorado, joining stores in Colorado Springs and Johnstown. The Littleton location will feature a 60-foot hubless Ferris wheel, Rollerball bowling lanes and a 16,000-gallon saltwater aquarium. Costco has also committed to the Mineral Place development.

stories.headline: Colorado's Jason Crow leads House passage of Iran war powers resolution for third time
stories.summary:
The U.S. House passed a resolution Wednesday directing President Donald Trump to end hostilities with Iran, the third time such a measure has cleared the chamber. The vote was 220-204, with seven Republicans breaking from party leadership, including three who had not previously supported the measure.

Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., was the driving force behind the resolution and pledged to continue forcing votes on the issue. "We're not going to stop," Crow said, adding that opposition to the war is "one of the most bipartisan issues in America." The conflict is now in its seventh month, and the Congressional Budget Office estimates it has cost more than $38 billion as of Aug. 1, with monthly costs running between $2 billion and $3 billion.

None of the three resolutions have reached the president's desk, and Trump would be expected to veto any such measure. The vote came the same day Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over his role in the Iran conflict.

A separate Ipsos poll released in April found that 71% of Americans believe the United States should not be involved in Iran. The CBO projected the war will push inflation 0.5 percentage points higher than expected heading into 2027.

stories.headline: Trump administration move to open federal lands to off-road vehicles draws cheers, concern in Colorado
stories.summary:
The U.S. Forest Service, under the Trump administration, is proposing to reverse a two-decade-old default that restricts off-road vehicles on federal roads and trails. Under the proposed change, published as a Federal Register notice, roads and trails on nearly 200 million acres of national forest would be presumed open to Jeeps, dirt bikes and other ATVs unless specific protections are carved out through negotiation or legal action.

The shift follows the administration's earlier rescission of the 25-year-old Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Colorado's separately negotiated roadless rule exemption will remain in place, according to administration officials, but environmental groups warn the broader change will degrade landscapes and disturb wildlife across the state's vast federal lands.

"Some places in our national forests are meant for quiet, undisturbed recreation and protecting sensitive wildlife, including endangered species," said Thomas Delehanty, senior attorney with Earthjustice's Rocky Mountain office. Off-road advocates counter that only 2,800 of Colorado's 28,000 miles of singletrack are currently open to motorized vehicles, calling the proposed change a long-overdue correction.

The rule change could take effect as early as 2028, setting up legal and legislative battles. Vehicle clubs and conservation groups in Colorado are already preparing their responses as the Forest Service begins the formal rulemaking process.

stories.headline: Lakewood man fatally shot at Green Mountain home in possible self-defense case
stories.summary:
A 45-year-old Lakewood man was shot and killed Tuesday afternoon at a residence in the Green Mountain neighborhood, and police say the shooting may have been an act of self-defense. Officers responded to the 1500 block of South Wright Street at 4:30 p.m. and found Mark Andrew Reins, who was transported to a hospital where he was pronounced dead.

Lakewood police identified the shooter and said that person is cooperating with investigators. "There is no threat to the public," department officials said in a news release Wednesday, adding that the investigation remains open.

Further details about the circumstances leading to the shooting were not immediately released. The case will be reviewed to determine whether self-defense statutes apply.

stories.headline: Boulder police search for missing woman, newborn believed to be traveling through south metro Denver
stories.summary:
Boulder police issued a missing persons alert Wednesday for a 24-year-old woman last seen Tuesday afternoon near Pine Street in Boulder, expressing concern for her safety and that of her eight-day-old son. Kylie Rucker is believed to be with the infant, Julio, and the child's father, 35-year-old Julio Cardona III, in a 2018 gray Subaru Forester with Colorado plate CYM-A61.

The vehicle was last spotted traveling southbound on Interstate 25 near Lone Tree just after noon Wednesday, placing it in the south Denver metro area. Police described Rucker as white, 5 feet 2 inches tall and 90 pounds with brown hair and brown eyes; Cardona is described as white, 5 feet 9 inches and 125 pounds with brown hair and hazel eyes.

The Colorado Bureau of Investigation issued the alert on behalf of Boulder police. Anyone with information is asked to call 911 or the Boulder Police Department at 303-441-3333.

stories.headline: Four new Denver restaurants set to open before year's end, including a RiNo pizzeria and Capitol Hill ice creamery
stories.summary:
Four notable Denver restaurants are expected to open their doors before the end of 2026, offering a range of cuisines from farm-to-table to Neapolitan-style pizza. Holm, a farm-to-table concept from the Paired Hospitality group — which also operates Major Tom and Michelin-starred Beckon — is set to open in late October at 609 Corona St., the longtime home of Table 6.

Risica, an Italian pizzeria from Naples-trained chef Andrea Frizzi, is targeting a late September or early October debut at 3463 Walnut St. in RiNo. The 2,100-square-foot space will feature a rotating brick oven for Milan-style pizza. Also in September, Sadboy Creamery, a cult-favorite ice cream pop-up, opens a permanent storefront at 1201 E. Colfax Ave. in Capitol Hill, with a grand opening set for Sept. 19.

The Stockton, an upscale steakhouse from Boulder restaurateur Bryan Dayton and executive chef Samuel McCandless, is planned for November inside the renovated Livestock Exchange Building at the National Western Center. The restaurant will source most of its beef from Dayton and McCandless's own cattle operation.

stories.headline: Broncos, Bo Nix struggle in offensive coordinator Webb's debut as play caller
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos and quarterback Bo Nix had a difficult outing under new offensive coordinator Zach Webb in his debut as play caller, according to NFL.com reporting on the team's early-season performance. The game represented a significant transition for Denver's offense as Webb takes over play-calling duties.

The Broncos' season-opening loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, 31-10 on Monday Night Football, underscored the offensive challenges facing the team as it adjusts to a new system. Nix, entering his second NFL season, is central to whether the new scheme can generate more production.

The result leaves Denver searching for answers on offense heading into Week 2, with questions about scheme, execution and personnel continuing to surround the team's unit.

topStory.headline: 911 Outages Hit Multiple Canadian Provinces in Early-Morning Disruption
topStory.summary:
Widespread disruptions to 911 emergency telephone service struck multiple Canadian provinces in the early morning hours of Thursday, September 17, 2026, affecting residents in Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Manitoba. Police services across the affected regions warned the public that some callers, particularly those on cellular networks, may be unable to connect to emergency dispatchers, and urged residents to use non-emergency lines, landlines, or Wi-Fi calling as alternatives.

In Ontario, Toronto Police reported at 4:30 a.m. local time that their 911 line was unable to receive calls, while the Ontario Provincial Police issued warnings of intermittent outages across parts of the province. Durham Regional Police, along with forces in Kingston, Peel, and York regions, reported similar problems. By approximately 6 a.m., many services confirmed their lines were being restored, though the OPP was still reporting issues as late as 7:30 a.m. and said it was working with service providers to expedite full restoration.

In Quebec, the Sûreté du Québec attributed the disruption to a technical issue affecting the transfer of certain calls. Montreal police confirmed they were affected but said service was restored by 4:45 a.m., with Quebec City police and other municipal forces reporting similar timelines. Nova Scotia officials issued a province-wide emergency alert describing the outages as intermittent and affecting parts of Canada broadly, advising residents to seek help directly from nearby police, fire, or medical facilities if 911 remained unavailable. New Brunswick authorities indicated the problem may be related to telecommunications carrier networks.

The cause of the outages had not been officially confirmed as of the time of reporting, and Bell Canada had been contacted for comment but had not yet responded. Authorities emphasized that emergency officers continued to respond to calls for service despite the disruption, and warned the public not to call 911 simply to test the line or seek updates. Investigators and service providers were working to determine the origin of the failure and restore full service across all affected regions.
